cards.title: The Delicate Dance: Keep Supply Under Demand
cards.summary: Manage the ratio of satisfied desire to unmet desire so demand stays ravenous and each launch sells out.
cards.use_when: Planning recurring promos, product drops or cohort launches and deciding how many units, SKUs or spots to release for an ecommerce brand.
steps: Recognize that demand is fractal, not linear: the source frames roughly one fifth of prospects as potentially willing to pay five times the price or more. A group of ten at $500 may include two willing to pay $5,000, so selling fewer units at a higher price can mean more profit, more value delivered and less cost.
Deliberately leave desire unsatisfied: cap supply below what you could sell so buyers who miss out carry pent-up desire into the next launch and act with more urgency.

Expect compounding effects on the next promotion: onlookers who see sold-out status and happy buyers want in more, and new prospects outside the original pool enter. Example sequence: open three spots at the higher price after selling out the previous round and fill them, still leaving unmet demand.

Avoid the opposite trap: re-promoting a fully-satisfied offer (e.g. the $500 tier everyone already bought) typically sells fewer slots each time, eventually drying up. The source frames this as the root of businesses constantly scrambling for fresh demand.
Internalize the stated principle: the longer you delay the ask, the bigger the ask you can make — a longer runway allows a bigger plane to take off.
Balance the extremes: zero supply earns nothing and eventually feels like rejection, and satisfying all demand kills the golden goose.
caveats: This is the source's framing (demand is fractal), not a measured law; treat the 20%/5x ratio as an illustrative pattern.
Under-supplying is a long-game strategy that deliberately forgoes near-term revenue.
The source notes people tolerate rejection from a brand far longer than most owners assume, but this is his experience, not a guarantee.

cards.title: How Premium Prices Are Actually Made: Scarcity of Solvers
cards.summary: Price power comes from buyers perceiving very few people who can solve their specialized problem, combined with the value of the outcome.
cards.use_when: Positioning a high-ticket product, service or premium tier, or explaining why cheaper competitors are not real alternatives for your customer.
steps: Diagnose the buyer's situation: if the problem is rare and blocks their happiness, it consumes their attention; the more specialized the problem, the fewer available solvers. In extreme cases the buyer perceives supply = 1.

Compare problem specificity: many people can teach how to make $10,000/month; far fewer can address how to add $5M in profit without adding product lines. The source cites a real project he solved in 60 minutes by slightly altering a pricing model.

Factor in time-to-outcome: if a solution accelerates a goal by one or two years, or immediately yields hundreds of thousands or millions, its perceived value rises sharply. Paying $50,000 for a day that adds $500,000/month in revenue within three months is framed as an obvious ROI.

Accept that value and rarity compound: the client is paying for accumulated expertise and to skip the cost and time of errors, going straight to the good stuff faster and cheaper than figuring it out alone.
Note the leverage of not needing the sale: the source declined two $50,000/day offers because his business already made more per day. The side that needs the exchange less has the upper hand.
caveats: The $50,000/day and $5M examples are the author's personal case studies, not benchmarks for other businesses.
Perceived scarcity can be implied by authority or fame, but manufacturing a false supply=1 claim is misrepresentation.
High-ticket day rates depend on the buyer's economics; a $500k/month revenue lift is not a typical or promised outcome.

cards.title: Creating Scarcity with Limited Releases and Public Sellouts
cards.summary: Cap physical product runs, sell out consistently, and broadcast the sellout to compound desire over time.
cards.use_when: Running limited-edition, seasonal or flavor/variant product drops for a physical-goods ecommerce brand.
steps: Pick the axis of limitation: flavor, color, design, size or quantity, e.g. this month we release 100 boxes of mint chocolate cookie protein bars.
Deliberately make fewer than you believe you can sell so you reliably sell out. The source states it is better to sell out consistently than to over-order and fail to create scarcity.

Announce the sellout publicly. Fence-sitters see social proof that others judged it worth buying, and the decision is taken away from them, which increases desire and makes them far more likely to buy the next drop.
Repeat on a cadence, but not too often: roughly once a month is the sweet spot among companies the source knows that do this regularly.

Study Chanel as the reference model: sending only one to two of each piece per store means every store carries a different selection and each item is the last or second-to-last in stock, supporting margins far above market over a century.
caveats: This is a compounding strategy only if you actually sell out; a failed limited run undercuts credibility.
Overusing drops dilutes the effect; the source warns against too-frequent releases.
The Chanel analogy is a brand observation, not a replicable tactic for every business.

cards.title: Four Ethical Scarcity Structures for Services
cards.summary: Use total-cap, weekly-cap, cohort-cap or no-reentry scarcity to raise take rates on service offers without being phony.
cards.use_when: Selling ongoing services, retainers or high-touch tiers where a fixed quantity of clients is genuinely serviceable.
steps: Total business cap: publicly commit to accepting X clients total at a service level, maintain a waiting list, and let prospects jump in the moment a door opens. The source reports price resistance disappears. Periodically raise capacity by 10-20% and re-cap, or raise prices and squeeze out lower-performing accounts.
Growth rate cap: state how many new clients you accept per week and how many spots remain, e.g. we take 5 per week, 3 are taken. This works because you genuinely can only onboard so many at once.
Cohort cap: accept X clients per class or cohort on whatever cadence you choose, monthly, quarterly or four times a year. This also creates operational cadence for onboarding.

Use scarcity for higher-ticket upsells: workshops, trainings, events, seminars and consulting naturally take time and grant access, so fixed seats or spots rapidly drive demand. Always have fewer spots than you think you can sell so the sellout is remembered.

Honest scarcity is the most ethical version: define a number you are genuinely willing to take on, then advertise it. Telling people you are three-quarters full for the week moves fence-sitters, and capacity itself implies social proof.
caveats: The source insists these only work ethically when the limit is real, or when it is a limit you define and honour.
Waiting-list and re-cap mechanics require disciplined delivery capacity.
Cohort cadence is more powerful the less frequently you start clients, but slower cadences defer revenue.

cards.title: Extreme Scarcity: Selling Capped 1-on-1 Access
cards.summary: Create a very high-priced, tightly capped access tier to a person and announce it, for outsized short-term revenue.
cards.use_when: Designing a premium tier, advisory or VIP access level where a founder's personal time is the product.
steps: Choose the access medium that fits how you actually like working, such as direct messages, email, phone, voice memos or Zoom calls. The source hates email and messages but does not mind Zoom, so he limits delivery to what he does not resent.
Cap the tier at a tiny number of clients and price it very high, then tell people it exists.
Keep delivery unscalable on purpose: the source says this is the fastest way he knows to make a lot of money, and that these tend to be some of the best clients.

Consider a no-reentry rule: once a client leaves the capped level, they can never return. He first used this with his gyms, then in a mastermind, then in a higher level of Gym Lords. It works best with small groups and loses teeth as groups get much bigger.
Accept that the 1% of 1% of prospects will adjust and take action; you are not trying to convert everyone.
caveats: The source explicitly calls this unscalable and says the pricing can exceed what you thought possible; treat as a strategy for a narrow tier, not the whole business.
He does not recommend it for people who hate the delivery burden of personal access.
No-reentry clauses weaken as the group scales up.

cards.title: Urgency Basics: Deadlines Drive Decisions
cards.summary: Scarcity limits quantity; urgency limits time, so a defined cutoff creates action without changing the offer.
cards.use_when: Adding a time-based mechanism to a product drop, bundle promotion or sales conversation that currently has no deadline.
steps: Separate the two levers: scarcity is a function of quantity; urgency is a function of time. Use them together often, but design them deliberately and separately.
Defined deadlines or cutoffs for purchase create urgency; the source calls deadlines the driver of decisions.
Choose from his four preferred ethical mechanisms: rolling cohorts, rolling seasonal urgency, promotional/pricing urgency, and exploding opportunity.

Expect the effect to concentrate at the end: on week-long campaigns or launches, the biggest sales come in the last four hours of the last day, up to 50-60% of sales in the final 3% of the time allotted, which he calls illogical but unmistakably human.

Do not fear turning away late buyers: the source says the fear of losing sales is unfounded because people who miss the deadline rarely would have bought even with pressure. Satisfy the many who act instead of mourning the few who never would have.
caveats: His 50-60% figure comes from observing launches; treat it as a pattern, not a rule for every campaign.
Fake deadlines destroy credibility; the source is explicit that countdowns must be real.
Much of this section is written for services and info products; the ecommerce translation is applying a genuine cutoff to a drop, bundle or promotion.

cards.title: Rolling Cohort Urgency for Services and Courses
cards.summary: Start clients on a fixed cadence so every prospect has a reason to buy today instead of waiting a week or a quarter.
cards.use_when: Running an onboarding, course, group program or service with recurring start dates.
steps: Set a regular kickoff cadence, weekly, biweekly, monthly or quarterly, and tell prospects what signing up today means: sign up today and you are in Monday's group, otherwise you wait until the next start date.

Add a small concrete nudge: mention a specific opening from a dropout, e.g. a client from a few weeks ago dropped out, so I have an opening for Monday's cohort; if you are going to do this sooner or later, might as well start now at the same price.
Recognize the corollary: the less frequently you start clients, the stronger the urgency. Twice a year is very powerful as the date approaches; every other week still confers a nudge.

Handle a buyer who wants in right after a cohort started: either offer a speedy personalized onboarding as a sign-up-today bonus to get them in, or, his preference, explain the advantages of waiting, such as more time to review materials and talk to employees (B2B) or family (B2C), plus an extended payment plan available only to them because the start date is far out.
Remember who controls the cadence: you always have the advantage because you are the one who calls the shots.
Treat cohort cadence as operational infrastructure too; it forces a choreographed onboarding experience that matters more as you scale.
caveats: Longer gaps between starts create stronger urgency but slower cash flow.
The extended-payment-plan and bonus onboarding offers are inducements; only promise terms you will honour.
This is a services/education pattern; ecommerce equivalents are launch windows or scheduled restocks.

cards.title: Seasonal and Promotional Urgency Wrappers
cards.summary: Give the same core offer a dated seasonal name and real deadline so it reads as a limited window.
cards.use_when: Ecommerce or local promotions that need novelty without changing the underlying product or service.
steps: Put the real promotion dates on landing pages and in copy, and make them visible everywhere. If the dates are not real, you lose credibility and look like every other wannabe marketer.

Rename the same core promotion by season to create a genuine start and finish, e.g. New Year Promotion ends Jan 30, Valentines Lovers Promo ends Feb 28, Sexy By Spring Special ends March 31, Fools in Love April Promo ends April 30.
Fire up a new ad campaign and landing page with new dates when the old one ends. The source says this takes about five minutes of editing and produces a large conversion lift.
For local businesses, use this as the number-one strategy: vary marketing more frequently than national advertisers, since a new dated wrapper on the same core service adds urgency and novelty.

Use pricing or bonus-based urgency instead of a service cutoff when you sell year round: let's start today to get the discount you came in for; we change them every four weeks and this is one of the better ones. The risk is missing the promotion, not the service.
Swap among pricing promotions, discounts, free install, free onboarding or an added workshop (e.g. valued at $1,000) to create urgency around interchangeable parts.
When genuinely raising prices, announce it: the price is going up, get in now. He says never raise prices silently, as it signals strength and flushes fence-sitters out of the pipeline.
caveats: The source warns that fake countdowns cost credibility; the deadline must be enforceable.
Promo/bonus urgency keeps integrity only if you frame it as the promotion ending, not a lie that you will refuse service after the date.
He frames pipeline-clearing price-rise announcements as a cash injection from already-warm leads; do not use them as a substitute for real pricing changes.

cards.title: Exploding Opportunity Urgency
cards.summary: When the value itself decays with time, make the ticking clock explicit and push for fast decisions.
cards.use_when: Offering an arbitrage, market inefficiency, early-vendor access or platform play whose returns shrink the longer the buyer waits.
steps: Identify whether the opportunity is time-decaying: market inefficiencies correct over time, so acting sooner matters disproportionately. The source's examples include buying goods on eBay to resell on Amazon, trading crypto, buying a stock, and getting into a new advertising platform before competitors pile in.
Emphasize the decay explicitly in the pitch; the whole point is that every second of delay costs disproportionate gains.

Recognize the same shape in talent markets: exploding offers in competitive hiring environments decrease pay or bonuses each day the candidate waits, forcing a fast decision instead of waiting for a better offer.
Frame your own offer the same way when the mechanism is real, so the prospect decides now rather than trying to time you out.
caveats: Only use this when the opportunity genuinely decays; inventing a clock is the credibility-destroying pattern the source criticizes elsewhere.
Arbitrage windows are examples of decay, not a promise that any specific window will remain open or profitable.
This is a services/information-play pattern; ecommerce uses include early-vendor access or platform-specific ad arbitrage.

cards.title: Bonus Stacks Beat Discounts: Expanding Price-to-Value Discrepancy
cards.summary: Break one offer into named component parts and stack them as bonuses, increasing perceived value rather than cutting price.
cards.use_when: Structuring how a product or service is presented and closing deals where prospects are hesitating on price.
steps: Accept the core premise: a single offer is less valuable than the same offer broken into component parts and stacked as bonuses. Until you enumerate what you actually do, those pieces are unknown to the buyer.

Anchor the price to the core offer, then layer increasingly valuable bonuses so the price-to-value discrepancy grows until it is too big to bear. Classic infomercials sell one knife for $38.95 then pile on 37 knives, sharpeners, pans and guarantees to beat the prospect into submission.

Never discount the main offer to close a deal; it teaches customers that your prices are negotiable, which the source calls terrible. Add bonuses instead: a position of strength and goodwill rather than weakness.
Watch what the infomercial formula does right: it establishes the price, then expands on it until passing feels stupid.
caveats: Bonuses inflate perceived value; the source explicitly notes the implication that the main thing must be worth more than the bonuses is psychological bias, not necessarily true.
Do not state bonus values you cannot justify with a real cost or comparison.
Discounting is sometimes the commercially rational choice; this is a strong opinion in the source, not a universal prohibition.

cards.title: Bonus Presentation Rules and the 11-Point Checklist
cards.summary: Name, justify, prove and visualize each bonus, and make its value eclipse the core offer.
cards.use_when: Writing sales copy, webinar slides or a 1-on-1 pitch that includes bonus deliverables.
steps: Always offer bonuses. Give each a special name with a benefit in the title.

For each bonus, tell them how it relates to their issue, what it is, how you discovered it or what you had to do to create it, and how it will make their experience faster, easier or less effort (the value equation).
Provide proof of value: a stat, a past client or personal experience.
Paint a vivid mental image of their life already having used the bonus and reaping the benefits.
Always ascribe a price tag and justify it.
Prefer tools and checklists over additional trainings because effort and time are lower for the buyer, so value is higher.
Make each bonus answer a specific objection in the prospect's mind about why they cannot or will not succeed; the bonus should prove the belief incorrect.
Also address what they will logically realize they need next: solve their next problem before they encounter it.
Let the bonuses' stated value eclipse the core offer; each addition widens the price-to-value gap and subconsciously implies the main offer is worth more.

Add scarcity or urgency to the bonuses themselves to put the technique on steroids, e.g. only buyers of XYZ program get Bonus 1-3, or three tickets left to a $5,000 virtual event included as a bonus, or a $1,000 bonus free only if you buy today.

For what belongs in the bonus vs. the core: pick the wow factor, items you would not want anyone to miss. Short, high-quality assets like checklists or infographics can be worth much more as a bonus than buried inside the core.
caveats: Scarcity on bonuses is quantity-based (never available elsewhere); urgency on bonuses is time-based (only if you buy today). The source flags the subtle difference as worth noting.
The implied bonuses-prove-the-core-is-worth-more logic is psychological positioning, not arithmetic.
Price tags on bonuses should reflect real costs or genuine market comparisons.

cards.title: Sequencing Bonuses in 1-on-1 Selling
cards.summary: Ask for the sale first; use bonuses after a no to match the specific objection, then ask again.
cards.use_when: Closing service or high-ticket deals where prospects raise objections and no group pitch is involved.
steps: When selling one on one, ask for the sale before presenting bonuses.
If they say yes, reveal the additional bonuses after they have signed up. This creates a wow experience and reinforces the decision.

If they say no, present a bonus that matches their perceived obstacle, then ask again. Do not feel weird about asking again: agree with the prospect, add the bonus, and ask whether this is fair enough.
Lean on reciprocity: people have a hard time rejecting it. Add a bonus to accommodate, then another, then another, and they feel almost obligated to buy.

This is why the deliverables from the Trim and Stack exercise are weaponized one at a time at the perfect moment: you were going to provide them anyway, but layering them one at a time increases perceived value.
caveats: The bonus must map to the stated objection or it reads as a random add-on.
The source notes group selling is beyond scope, so this sequencing is specifically 1-on-1.
Repeated re-asks rely on reciprocity; aggressive use may suit some audiences poorly.

cards.title: Sourcing Bonus Assets and Partner Discounts
cards.summary: Build a vault of one-time-created assets and negotiate adjacent-business bonuses with referral commissions.
cards.use_when: Creating future bonus inventory and building a partner network whose products solve what your customers need next.
steps: Create checklists, tools, swipe files, scripts and templates, anything that takes lots of time and effort to create once but is easy for the buyer to use and can be given away endlessly.
Record every workshop, webinar, event and interview; keep them in a vault to deploy later against a specific perceived obstacle.

Go to adjacent businesses that solve needs your customer will have as a result of starting with you, and negotiate group discounts and a referral commission. You negotiate with the purchasing power of all your customers at once, which is very powerful.

Worked example: a $400 pain-clinic offer can include 1-2 free massages, two chiropractic adjustments ($100), an anti-inflammatory food discount ($50 savings), braces/orthotics discounts ($150), a free training session and pool month ($100), and pharmacy discounts ($100/month). Stack these across multiple providers, such as ten chiropractors each contributing an adjustment, and the bonuses alone can exceed the $400 price.

Then negotiate affiliate commissions on the same intros: the chiropractor pays $100 per new patient, orthotics $100 per referral, the health club $50 per signup or a free membership, the pharmacy $100 per person. On the example, a $400 offer can generate an extra $350 in pure profit on customers you already paid to acquire.

Use high-perceived-value, low-cost vehicles where they fit: information products (extra login only), tickets to virtual events and experiences, and fixed-cost VIP service for a month, which also doubles as an upsell path.
caveats: Partners must not be direct competitors.
The source's $350 extra-profit figure is an illustrative calculation, not a forecast.
These bonuses solve needs triggered by your offer; mismatched partners dilute trust.
In ecommerce, verify the current terms of any affiliate or referral arrangement before committing.

cards.title: Risk Reversal Math: Why Stronger Guarantees Usually Net More
cards.summary: Model the sales lift against the refund increase before rejecting a strong guarantee on emotion.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to strengthen a product guarantee and how much refund risk an ecommerce offer can absorb.
steps: Start from the premise that risk, that the product does not do what it should for the buyer, is the single greatest objection, so reversing it immediately makes any offer more attractive. The source says Jason Fladlien reported conversion on an offer rising 2-4x simply by changing the quality of the guarantee.

Run the arithmetic before deciding: baseline of 100 sales with 5 refunds (5%) nets 95. With the stronger guarantee, 130 sales and 13 refunds (10%) nets 117, which is 1.23x, a 23% increase all to the bottom line. Doubling the refund rate still produced more net sales.

Note the break-even condition: for a guarantee to be unprofitable, the absolute increase in sales would have to be fully offset by an absolute increase in refunds; e.g. a 5-point absolute sales increase offset by a 5-point absolute refund increase, which would mean the refund rate doubled.
Heed the warning: people who buy only because of a guarantee can be poor customers who may not do the work. Tie the guarantee to the actions they need for success so all parties win.
If your cost of fulfilment is high, use a conditional or anti-guarantee rather than an unconditional one, otherwise you eat both the refund and the cost of delivering.
Always state your guarantee hard, even if you have none: say it boldly and give the reason why.
caveats: The 2-4x conversion figure is attributed to another practitioner's experience, not a universal result.
Consumer entitlement and shifting norms make unconditional guarantees riskier over time.
Guarantee mechanics are jurisdiction-specific for ecommerce; check legal requirements before advertising refund terms.

cards.title: The Four Guarantee Types and How to Choose
cards.summary: Unconditional, conditional, anti- and implied guarantees each fit different ticket sizes, cost structures and business models.
cards.use_when: Designing the risk-reversal clause for an ecommerce offer, especially deciding between broad refunds and outcome-based terms.
steps: Unconditional: the strongest form, effectively a pay-first trial. It gets many more people to buy but produces some refunds. Example client outcomes include full refund, 50% refund, refund of ad spend plus ancillary costs, paying for a competitor's program instead, or returning money plus an additional $1,000.

Conditional: includes terms and conditions and is where you can get very creative. Aim for better than money-back: match their investment with an equal or higher perceived commitment. Build the key success actions into the conditions, with the ideal that 100% of customers qualify but achieve the result and never want the refund. Given the choice between a refund and the promised outcome, the vast majority take the outcome.

Anti-guarantee: explicitly all sales are final, owned confidently with a creative reason why that shows a massive exposure or vulnerability the buyer instantly understands. Especially important for consumables or items that massively diminish in value once delivered.

Implied guarantee: any performance-based offer, such as revshare, profitshare, triggers, ratchets or monetary bonuses. If I do not perform, I do not get paid; if I do a great job, I am very well compensated. Requires transparency in measuring the outcome and trust or control that you will actually be compensated.

Match guarantee breadth to business type: bigger, broader guarantees work better in lower-ticket B2C (many buyers will not bother pursuing a refund); higher ticket and more business-oriented offers should steer toward specific guarantees, with or without refunds and conditions.

Give the guarantee teeth with the conditional formula: If you do not get X result in Y time period, we will Z. Without the or-what portion it sounds weak. You will get 20 clients in your first 30 days, or we give you your money back plus your advertising spend with us is strong.
Name the guarantee something memorable rather than satisfaction, e.g. in 30 days, if you would not jump into shark-infested waters to get our product back, we will return every dollar you paid.
caveats: The source says the more conditions you add to an unconditional guarantee, the faster it loses its teeth; conditions and unconditional power trade off.
Anti-guarantees need a believable reason why, or they read as mere policy.
Implied guarantees only work where outcomes are measurable and payment is enforceable.
Guarantee language must comply with local consumer law; verify before publishing.

cards.title: Conditional Guarantee Variants: Service, Modified Service and Credit
cards.summary: Use outcome-based guarantees that keep clients working toward the result while limiting your exposure.
cards.use_when: Choosing a conditional guarantee structure for coaching, services or programs where you can keep delivering until the outcome is met.
steps: Service guarantee: keep working for them free until X is achieved. The source calls it his personal favourite because it guarantees the goal while eliminating the time element, so you are never at risk of losing the money. Make it conditional on key success actions: setting up a web page, attending calls, showing up to workouts, weighing in, reporting data. He reports that since advising businesses to use it, not a single client has taken one up; in practice either you happily keep working with a committed client to the result, or it quietly drops because the client is close enough to satisfied and the sales conversation is months in the past.

Modified service guarantee: give another Y-long period of service or access free, where Y is generally at least twice the original duration. This ties a specific duration to your extended involvement instead of being on the hook forever, a good starting point before the all-out service guarantee.
Credit-based guarantee: give back what they paid, but as credit toward any service you offer.

Outsized refund guarantee: double or triple their money back, or a no-strings payment far above the price, attached to a consumption condition. Fladlien's example: spend $X on ads using the course methods and if you do not make money, he buys the store for $25,000. He attributed an extra $3M in sales to it on a $2,997 course and only paid out 10 of the $25,000 refunds. This fits high-margin offers and situations where a lot must be done by the buyer and, if done, results are highly likely.
caveats: Outsized refund guarantees depend on high margins and a genuinely low chance of failure when conditions are met; the $25,000 payout is a case study, not a template for your economics.
The nobody-claims-the-service-guarantee observation is the source's experience, not a statistical expectation.
Consumption conditions should reflect actions genuinely required for success, not gimmicks designed to disqualify buyers.

cards.title: Stacking Guarantees for Compounded Risk Reversal
cards.summary: Layer different guarantee types to remove risk sequentially and future-pace the buyer toward the outcome.
cards.use_when: Building a premium or high-ticket offer where a single guarantee is not enough to overcome hesitation.
steps: Layer an unconditional guarantee on top of a conditional one, e.g. a 30-day no-questions-asked refund plus a conditional triple-your-money-back 90-day guarantee.

Stack two conditional guarantees around sequential outcomes: you will make $10,000 by 60 days and $30,000 by 90 days, provided you do things 1, 2 and 3. Spelling out the conditional timeline future-paces the prospect into an outcome they now believe is far more likely.
Treat stacking as evidence you are serious about client results and convinced they will get them; it shifts risk from the buyer back onto you.
caveats: Stacked guarantees multiply your worst-case exposure; model the refund arithmetic from the risk-reversal math card before committing.
Future-pacing with specific dollar milestones sets expectations you must be prepared to honour.

cards.title: Crafting and Delivering an Unconditional Refund Guarantee
cards.summary: Pitch the strongest refund guarantee by removing the decision from today and promising to keep only happy money.
cards.use_when: Writing or delivering the guarantee portion of a webinar, sales page or closing conversation for a lower-ticket B2C offer.
steps: Remove the immediate yes/no: I am not asking you to decide yes or no today, I am asking you to make a fully informed decision. Use the house analogy: you do not buy a house without looking inside, so get inside the program, verify the claims, and decide then.

Echo the source's phrasing: whether it is 29 minutes or 29 days from now, if you ain't happy, I ain't happy. For any reason whatsoever, they can get the money back by emailing support with a simple request.
Back the promise with concrete support metrics if you have them; the original script cited average response times of 61 minutes over a 24/7 period.

Use a satisfaction-based guarantee with a best-case/worst-case close. Weight-loss program example: best case you get the body of your dreams; worst case you tell me I suck, I write you a check, and you get six weeks of free training. He reports two people took him up on it out of 4,000 sales over three and a half years.

If you use satisfaction-based refunds, be genuinely good at fulfilment; the source credits the guarantee with a lot of closed deals but warns the model is riskier as ticket size and fulfilment cost rise.
caveats: Satisfaction/no-questions-asked is the highest form of guarantee because the buyer could ask for a refund even when you did everything right; the source says this works much better in lower-ticket situations.
His 2-in-4,000 refund rate is an example from his own business, not a benchmark.
Do not emit support response-time claims you cannot substantiate.

cards.title: Strengthening a Guarantee Through Naming and Wording
cards.summary: Give the guarantee a vivid, benefit-laden name and lead with the reason why, so it does not read as boilerplate.
cards.use_when: Finalising the wording and branding of a guarantee for product pages, sales copy or checkout messaging.
steps: Replace vanilla terms like satisfaction with a stronger, more concrete description.
Generic example to avoid: 30 Day Money Back Satisfaction Guarantee.
Good creative imagery: In 30 days, if you would not jump into shark-infested waters to get our product back, we will return every dollar you paid.
Even stronger: the source's Club a Baby Seal Guarantee, where after 30 days of using the services, if you would not club a baby seal to stay on as a customer, you do not pay a penny.
Always name the guarantee and state it boldly, with the reason why, even if you choose not to offer one.
caveats: The source's extreme imagery examples are intentionally provocative; tone must fit your brand and audience.
Verify advertising and refund-wording compliance for your market before publishing the named guarantee.

cards.title: The Delicate Dance: Keep Supply Under Demand
cards.summary: Manage the ratio of satisfied desire to unmet desire so demand stays ravenous and each launch sells out.
cards.use_when: Planning recurring promotions, cohort launches or high-ticket services, and deciding how many units or spots to release.
steps: Recognize that demand is fractal (80/20-shaped), not linear: roughly one fifth of prospects may be willing to pay five times the price or more. A group of ten at $500 may include two willing to pay $5,000 — selling fewer units at the higher price can mean more profit, more value delivered and less cost.
Deliberately leave desire unsatisfied: cap supply below what you could sell, so buyers who miss out carry pent-up desire into the next launch and act with more urgency.

Expect compounding effects on the next promotion: onlookers who see sold-out status and happy buyers want in more, and new prospects outside the original pool enter. Example sequence: open three spots at the higher price after selling out the previous round and fill them — still leaving unmet demand.

Avoid the opposite trap: re-promoting a fully-satisfied offer (e.g. the $500 tier everyone already bought) typically sells fewer slots each time, eventually drying up. The source frames this as the root of businesses constantly scrambling for fresh demand.
Internalize the stated principle: "The longer you delay the ask, the bigger the ask you can make" — a longer runway allows a bigger plane to take off.
Balance the extremes: zero supply earns nothing and eventually feels like rejection (and takes longer than you expect for people to leave); satisfying all demand kills the golden goose.
caveats: This is the source's framing ('demand is fractal'), not a measured law; treat the 20%/5x ratio as an illustrative pattern.
Under-supplying is a long-game strategy — it deliberately forgoes near-term revenue.
The source notes people tolerate rejection from a brand far longer than most owners assume, but this is his experience, not a guarantee.

cards.title: How Premium Prices Are Actually Made: Scarcity of Solvers
cards.summary: Price power comes from buyers perceiving very few people who can solve their specialized problem, combined with the value of the outcome.
cards.use_when: Positioning high-ticket services or coaching, or explaining to a client why cheaper competitors are not real alternatives.
steps: Diagnose the buyer's situation: if the problem is rare and blocks their happiness, it consumes their attention; the more specialized the problem, the fewer available solvers. In extreme cases the buyer perceives supply = 1.

Compare problem specificity: many people can teach 'how to make $10,000/month'; far fewer can address 'how to add $5M in profit without adding product lines' — the source cites a real project he solved in 60 minutes by slightly altering a pricing model.

Factor in time-to-outcome: if a solution accelerates a goal by one or two years, or immediately yields hundreds of thousands or millions, its perceived value rises sharply. Paying $50,000 for a day that adds $500,000/month in revenue within three months is framed as an obvious ROI.

Accept that value and rarity compound: the client is paying for accumulated expertise and to skip the cost and time of errors — going straight to the good stuff faster and cheaper than figuring it out alone.

Note the leverage of not needing the sale: the source declined two $50,000/day offers because his business already made more per day. The side that needs the exchange less has the upper hand — a pricing and negotiation principle he says has served him best.
caveats: The $50,000/day and $5M examples are the author's personal case studies, not benchmarks for other businesses.
Perceived scarcity can be implied by authority or fame, but manufacturing a false supply=1 claim is misrepresentation.
High-ticket day rates depend on the buyer's economics; a $500k/month revenue lift is not a typical or promised outcome.

cards.title: Creating Scarcity with Limited Releases and Public Sellouts
cards.summary: Cap physical product runs, sell out consistently, and broadcast the sellout to compound desire over time.
cards.use_when: Running limited-edition or seasonal product drops for a physical-goods ecommerce brand.
steps: Pick the axis of limitation: flavor, color, design, size or quantity — e.g. 'this month we release 100 boxes of mint chocolate cookie protein bars.'
Deliberately make fewer than you believe you can sell, so you reliably sell out. The source states it is better to sell out consistently than to over-order and fail to create scarcity.

Announce the sellout publicly. Fence-sitters see social proof that others judged it worth buying, and the decision is taken away from them — which increases desire and makes them far more likely to buy the next drop.
Repeat on a cadence, but not too often: roughly once a month is the sweet spot among companies the source knows that do this regularly.

Study Chanel as the reference model: sending only one to two of each piece per store means every store carries a different selection and each item is the last or second-to-last in stock, supporting margins far above market over a century.
caveats: This is a compounding strategy only if you actually sell out — a failed 'limited' run undercuts credibility.
Overusing drops dilutes the effect; the source warns against too-frequent releases.
The Chanel analogy is a brand observation, not a replicable tactic for every business.

cards.title: Four Ethical Scarcity Structures for Services
cards.summary: Use total-cap, weekly-cap, cohort-cap or no-reentry scarcity to raise take rates on service offers without being phony.
cards.use_when: Selling ongoing services, agency retainers or high-touch tiers where a fixed quantity of clients is genuinely serviceable.
steps: Total business cap: publicly commit to accepting X clients total at a service level, maintain a waiting list, and let prospects jump in the moment a door opens — the source reports price resistance disappears. Periodically raise capacity by 10–20% and re-cap, or raise prices and squeeze out lower-performing accounts.

Growth rate cap: state how many new clients you accept per week and how many spots remain, e.g. 'we take 5 per week, 3 are taken, I have 6 more calls this week.' This works because you genuinely can only onboard so many at once.

Cohort cap: accept X clients per class or cohort on whatever cadence you choose — monthly, quarterly or four times a year. 'We take 100 clients 4 times a year; doors open then close.' This also creates operational cadence for onboarding.

Use scarcity for higher-ticket upsells: workshops, trainings, events, seminars and consulting naturally take time and grant access, so fixed seats or spots rapidly drive demand. Always have fewer spots than you think you can sell so the sellout is remembered.

Honest scarcity is the most ethical version: define a number you are genuinely willing to take on, then advertise it. Telling people you are 81% to capacity or three-quarters full for the week moves fence-sitters, and capacity itself implies social proof.
caveats: The source insists these only work ethically when the limit is real, or when it is a limit you define and honour.
Waiting-list and re-cap mechanics require disciplined delivery capacity.
Cohort cadence is more powerful the less frequently you start clients, but slower cadences defer revenue.

cards.title: Extreme Scarcity: Selling Capped 1-on-1 Access
cards.summary: Create a very high-priced, tightly capped access tier to a person and announce it, for outsized short-term revenue.
cards.use_when: Designing a premium tier, advisory or VIP access level where a founder's personal time is the product.
steps: Choose the access medium that fits how you actually like working — direct messages, email, phone, voice memos, Zoom calls. The source hates email and messages but does not mind Zoom, so he limits delivery to what he does not resent.
Cap the tier at a tiny number of clients and price it very high, then tell people it exists.
Keep delivery unscalable on purpose: the source says this is the fastest way he knows to make a lot of money, and that these tend to be some of the best clients.

Consider a no-reentry rule — once a client leaves the capped level, they can never return. He first used this with his gyms, then in a mastermind, then in a higher level of Gym Lords. It works best with small groups and loses teeth as groups get much bigger.
Accept that the '1% of 1%' of prospects will adjust and take action — you are not trying to convert everyone.
caveats: The source explicitly calls this unscalable and says the pricing can exceed what you thought possible — treat as a strategy for a narrow tier, not the whole business.
He does not recommend it for people who hate money's counterpart: the delivery burden of personal access.
No-reentry clauses weaken as the group scales up.

cards.title: Urgency Basics: Deadlines Drive Decisions
cards.summary: Scarcity limits quantity; urgency limits time — a defined cutoff creates action without changing the offer.
cards.use_when: Adding a time-based mechanism to a launch, promotion or sales conversation that currently has no deadline.
steps: Separate the two levers: scarcity is a function of quantity; urgency is a function of time. Use them together often, but design them deliberately and separately.
Defined deadlines or cutoffs for purchase create urgency — 'deadlines drive decisions' is the source's stated maxim.
Choose from his four preferred ethical mechanisms: rolling cohorts, rolling seasonal urgency, promotional/pricing urgency, and exploding opportunity.

Expect the effect to concentrate at the end: on week-long campaigns or launches, the biggest sales come in the last four hours of the last day — up to 50–60% of sales in the final 3% of the time allotted, which he calls illogical but unmistakably human.

Do not fear turning away late buyers: the source says the fear of losing sales is unfounded because people who miss the deadline rarely would have bought even with pressure. Satisfy the many who act instead of mourning the few who never would have.
caveats: His 50–60% figure comes from observing launches; treat it as a pattern, not a rule for every campaign.
Fake deadlines destroy credibility — the source is explicit that countdowns must be real.
Category scope note: much of this section is written for services and info products; the ecommerce translation is applying a genuine cutoff to a drop, bundle or promotion.

cards.title: Rolling Cohort Urgency for Services and Courses
cards.summary: Start clients on a fixed cadence so every prospect has a reason to buy today instead of waiting a week or a quarter.
cards.use_when: Running an onboarding, course, group program or service with recurring start dates.
steps: Set a regular kickoff cadence — weekly, biweekly, monthly or quarterly — and tell prospects what signing up today means: 'sign up today and you are in Monday's group, otherwise you wait until the next start date.'

Add a small concrete nudge: mention a specific opening from a dropout ('a client from a few weeks ago dropped out, so I have an opening for Monday's cohort; if you are going to do this sooner or later, might as well start now and reap the rewards sooner at the same price').
Recognize the corollary: the less frequently you start clients, the stronger the urgency — twice a year is very powerful as the date approaches; every other week still confers a nudge.

Handle a buyer who wants in right after a cohort started: either (a) offer a speedy personalized onboarding as a sign-up-today bonus to get them in, or (b) his preference — explain the advantages of waiting, such as more time to review materials and talk to employees (B2B) or family (B2C), plus an extended payment plan available only to them because the start date is far out.
Remember who controls the cadence: 'you always have the advantage because you are the one who calls the shots.'
Treat cohort cadence as operational infrastructure too — it forces a choreographed onboarding experience that matters more as you scale.
caveats: Longer gaps between starts create stronger urgency but slower cash flow.
The extended-payment-plan and bonus onboarding offers are inducements; only promise terms you will honour.
This is a services/education pattern; ecommerce equivalents are launch windows or scheduled restocks.

cards.title: Seasonal and Promotional Urgency Wrappers
cards.summary: Give the same core offer a dated seasonal name and real deadline so it reads as a limited window.
cards.use_when: Local or ecommerce promotions that need novelty without changing the underlying product or service.
steps: Put the real promotion dates on landing pages and in copy, and make them visible everywhere. If the dates are not real, you lose credibility and look like every other wannabe marketer.

Rename the same core promotion by season to create a genuine start and finish: 'New Year Promotion ends Jan 30', 'Valentines Lovers Promo ends Feb 28', 'Sexy By Spring Special ends March 31', 'Fools in Love April Promo ends April 30'.
Fire up a new ad campaign and landing page with new dates when the old one ends — the source says this takes about five minutes of editing and produces a large conversion lift.
For local businesses, use this as the number-one strategy: vary marketing more frequently than national advertisers, since a new dated wrapper on the same core service adds urgency and novelty.

Use pricing/bonus-based urgency instead of a service cutoff when you sell year round: 'let's start today to get the discount you came in for; we change them every four weeks and this is one of the better ones' — the risk is missing the promotion, not the service.
Swap among pricing promotions, discounts, free install, free onboarding or an added workshop (e.g. valued at $1,000) to create urgency around interchangeable parts.
When genuinely raising prices, announce it: 'The price is going up — get in now.' He says never raise prices silently, as it signals strength and flushes fence-sitters out of the pipeline.
caveats: The source warns that fake countdowns cost credibility; the deadline must be enforceable.
Promo/bonus urgency keeps integrity only if you frame it as the promotion ending, not a lie that you will refuse service after the date.
He frames pipeline-clearing price-rise announcements as a cash injection from already-warm leads — do not use them as a substitute for real pricing changes.

cards.title: Exploding Opportunity Urgency
cards.summary: When the value itself decays with time, make the ticking clock explicit and push for fast decisions.
cards.use_when: Offering an arbitrage, market inefficiency, early-access platform, or any opportunity whose returns shrink the longer the buyer waits.
steps: Identify whether the opportunity is time-decaying: market inefficiencies correct over time, so acting sooner matters disproportionately. The source's examples include buying goods on eBay to resell on Amazon, trading crypto, buying a stock, and getting into a new advertising platform before competitors pile in.
Emphasize the decay explicitly in the pitch — the whole point is that every second of delay costs disproportionate gains.

Recognize the same shape in talent markets: 'exploding offers' in competitive hiring environments decrease pay or bonuses each day the candidate waits, forcing a fast decision instead of waiting for a better offer.
Frame your own offer the same way when the mechanism is real, so the prospect decides now rather than trying to time you out.
caveats: Only use this when the opportunity genuinely decays — inventing a clock is the credibility-destroying pattern the source criticizes elsewhere.
Arbitrage windows are examples of decay, not a promise that any specific window will remain open or profitable.
This is a services/information-play pattern; ecommerce uses include early-vendor access or platform-specific ad arbitrage.

cards.title: Bonus Stacks Beat Discounts: Expanding Price-to-Value Discrepancy
cards.summary: Break one offer into named component parts and stack them as bonuses, increasing perceived value rather than cutting price.
cards.use_when: Structuring how a product or service is presented and closing deals where prospects are hesitating on price.
steps: Accept the core premise: a single offer is less valuable than the same offer broken into component parts and stacked as bonuses. Until you enumerate what you actually do, those pieces are unknown to the buyer.

Anchor the price to the core offer, then layer increasingly valuable bonuses so the price-to-value discrepancy grows until it is too big to bear. Classic infomercials sell one knife for $38.95 then pile on 37 knives, sharpeners, pans and guarantees to beat the prospect into submission.

Never discount the main offer to close a deal — it teaches customers that your prices are negotiable, which the source calls terrible. Add bonuses instead: a position of strength and goodwill rather than weakness.
Watch what the infomercial formula does right: it establishes the price, then expands on it until passing feels stupid.
caveats: Bonuses inflate perceived value; the source explicitly notes the implication 'the main thing must be worth more than the bonuses' is psychological bias, not necessarily true.
Do not state bonus values you cannot justify with a real cost or comparison.
Discounting is sometimes the commercially rational choice — this is a strong opinion in the source, not a universal prohibition.

cards.title: Bonus Presentation Rules and the 11-Point Checklist
cards.summary: Name, justify, prove and visualize each bonus, and make its value eclipse the core offer.
cards.use_when: Writing sales copy, webinar slides or a 1-on-1 pitch that includes bonus deliverables.
steps: Always offer bonuses. Give each a special name with a benefit in the title.

For each bonus, tell them: (a) how it relates to their issue, (b) what it is, (c) how you discovered it or what you had to do to create it, (d) how it will make their experience faster, easier or less effort (the value equation).
Provide proof of value — a stat, a past client or personal experience.
Paint a vivid mental image of their life already having used the bonus and reaping the benefits.
Always ascribe a price tag and justify it.
Prefer tools and checklists over additional trainings because effort and time are lower for the buyer, so value is higher.
Make each bonus answer a specific objection in the prospect's mind about why they cannot or will not succeed — the bonus should prove the belief incorrect.
Also address what they will logically realize they need next: solve their next problem before they encounter it.
Let the bonuses' stated value eclipse the core offer; each addition widens the price-to-value gap and subconsciously implies the main offer is worth more.

Add scarcity or urgency to the bonuses themselves to put the technique on steroids — e.g. only buyers of XYZ program get Bonus 1–3, or three tickets left to a $5,000 virtual event included as a bonus, or a $1,000 bonus free only if you buy today.

For what belongs in the bonus vs. the core: pick the 'wow factor' — items you would not want anyone to miss. Short, high-quality assets like checklists or infographics can be worth much more as a bonus than buried inside the core.
caveats: Scarcity on bonuses is quantity-based (never available elsewhere); urgency on bonuses is time-based (only if you buy today). The source flags the subtle difference as worth noting.
The implied 'bonuses prove the core is worth more' logic is psychological positioning, not arithmetic.
Price tags on bonuses should reflect real costs or genuine market comparisons.

cards.title: Sequencing Bonuses in 1-on-1 Selling
cards.summary: Ask for the sale first; use bonuses after a no to match the specific objection, then ask again.
cards.use_when: Closing service or high-ticket deals where prospects raise objections and no group pitch is involved.
steps: When selling one on one, ask for the sale before presenting bonuses.
If they say yes, reveal the additional bonuses after they have signed up. This creates a wow experience and reinforces the decision.

If they say no, present a bonus that matches their perceived obstacle, then ask again. Do not feel weird about asking again: agree with the prospect, add the bonus, and ask whether this is 'fair enough'.
Lean on reciprocity — people have a hard time rejecting it. Add a bonus to accommodate, then another, then another, and they feel almost obligated to buy.

This is why the deliverables from the 'Trim and Stack' exercise are weaponized one at a time at the perfect moment: you were going to provide them anyway, but layering them one at a time increases perceived value.
caveats: The bonus must map to the stated objection or it reads as a random add-on.
The source notes group selling is beyond the scope of this material, so this sequencing is specifically 1-on-1.
Repeated re-asks rely on reciprocity; aggressive use may suit some audiences poorly.

cards.title: Sourcing Bonus Assets and Partner Discounts
cards.summary: Build a vault of one-time-created assets and negotiate adjacent-business bonuses with referral commissions.
cards.use_when: Creating future bonus inventory and building a partner network whose products solve what your customers need next.
steps: Create checklists, tools, swipe files, scripts and templates — anything that takes lots of time and effort to create once but is easy for the buyer to use and can be given away endlessly.
Record every workshop, webinar, event and interview; keep them in a vault to deploy later against a specific perceived obstacle.

Go to adjacent businesses that solve needs your customer will have as a result of starting with you, and negotiate group discounts and a referral commission. You negotiate with the purchasing power of all your customers at once, which is very powerful.

Worked example: a $400 pain-clinic offer can include 1–2 free massages, two chiropractic adjustments ($100), an anti-inflammatory food discount ($50 savings), braces/orthotics discounts ($150), a free training session and pool month ($100), and pharmacy discounts ($100/mo). Stack these across multiple providers — e.g. ten chiropractors each contributing an adjustment — and the bonuses alone can exceed the $400 price.

Then negotiate affiliate commissions on the same intros: the chiropractor pays $100 per new patient, orthotics $100 per referral, the health club $50 per signup or a free membership, the pharmacy $100 per person. On the example, a $400 offer can generate an extra $350 — pure profit on customers you already paid to acquire.

Use high-perceived-value, low-cost vehicles where they fit: information products (extra login only), tickets to virtual events and experiences, and fixed-cost VIP service for a month — which also doubles as an upsell path.
caveats: Partners must not be direct competitors.
The source's $350 extra-profit figure is an illustrative calculation, not a forecast.
These bonuses solve needs triggered by your offer; mismatched partners dilute trust.
In ecommerce, verify the current interface and terms of any affiliate or referral arrangement before committing.

cards.title: Risk Reversal Math: Why Stronger Guarantees Usually Net More
cards.summary: Model the sales lift against the refund increase before rejecting a strong guarantee on emotion.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to strengthen a guarantee and how much refund risk you can absorb.
steps: Start from the premise that risk — that the product does not do what it should for the buyer — is the single greatest objection, so reversing it immediately makes any offer more attractive. The source says Jason Fladlien reported conversion on an offer rising 2–4x simply by changing the quality of the guarantee.

Run the arithmetic before deciding: baseline of 100 sales with 5 refunds (5%) nets 95. With the stronger guarantee, 130 sales and 13 refunds (10%) nets 117 — 1.23x, a 23% increase, all to the bottom line. Doubling the refund rate still produced more net sales.

Note the break-even condition: for a guarantee to be unprofitable, the absolute increase in sales would have to be fully offset by an absolute increase in refunds — e.g. a 5-point absolute sales increase offset by a 5-point absolute refund increase, which would mean the refund rate doubled.
Heed the warning: people who buy only because of a guarantee can be poor customers who may not do the work. Tie the guarantee to the actions they need for success so all parties win.
If your cost of fulfilment is high, use a conditional or anti-guarantee rather than an unconditional one — otherwise you eat both the refund and the cost of delivering.
Always state your guarantee hard, even if you have none: say it boldly and give the reason why.
caveats: The 2–4x conversion figure is attributed to another practitioner's experience, not a universal result.
Consumer entitlement and shifting norms make unconditional guarantees riskier over time.
Guarantee mechanics are jurisdiction-specific for ecommerce — check legal requirements before advertising refund terms.

cards.title: The Four Guarantee Types and How to Choose
cards.summary: Unconditional, conditional, anti- and implied guarantees each fit different ticket sizes, cost structures and business models.
cards.use_when: Designing the risk-reversal clause for an offer, especially deciding between broad refunds and outcome-based terms.
steps: Unconditional: the strongest form — effectively a pay-first trial. It gets many more people to buy but produces some refunds. Example client outcomes: full refund, 50% refund, refund of ad spend plus ancillary costs, you pay for a competitor's program instead, or you return the money plus an additional $1,000.

Conditional: includes terms and conditions and is where you can get very creative. Aim for 'better than money-back' — match their investment with an equal or higher perceived commitment. Build the key success actions into the conditions, with the ideal that 100% of customers qualify but achieve the result and never want the refund. Given the choice between a refund and the promised outcome, the vast majority take the outcome.

Anti-guarantee: explicitly 'all sales are final', owned confidently with a creative reason why that shows a massive exposure or vulnerability the buyer instantly understands. Especially important for consumables or items that massively diminish in value once delivered.

Implied guarantee: any performance-based offer — revshare, profitshare, triggers, ratchets, monetary bonuses. If I do not perform, I do not get paid; if I do a great job, I am very well compensated. Requires transparency in measuring the outcome and trust or control that you will actually be compensated.

Match guarantee breadth to business type: bigger, broader guarantees work better in lower-ticket B2C (many buyers will not bother pursuing a refund); higher ticket and more business-oriented offers should steer toward specific guarantees, with or without refunds and conditions.

Give the guarantee teeth with the conditional formula: 'If you do not get X result in Y time period, we will Z.' Without the 'or what' portion it sounds weak — 'we will get you 20 clients guaranteed' is weak; 'you will get 20 clients in your first 30 days, or we give you your money back plus your advertising spend with us' is strong.
Name the guarantee something memorable rather than 'satisfaction': e.g. 'in 30 days, if you would not jump into shark-infested waters to get our product back, we will return every dollar you paid.'
caveats: The source says the more conditions you add to an unconditional guarantee, the faster it loses its teeth — conditions and unconditional power trade off.
Anti-guarantees need a believable reason why, or they read as mere policy.
Implied guarantees only work where outcomes are measurable and payment is enforceable.
Guarantee language must comply with local consumer law — verify before publishing.

cards.title: Conditional Guarantee Variants: Service, Modified Service and Credit
cards.summary: Use outcome-based guarantees that keep clients working toward the result while limiting your exposure.
cards.use_when: Choosing a conditional guarantee structure for coaching, services or programs where you can keep delivering until the outcome is met.
steps: Service guarantee: keep working for them free until X is achieved. The source calls it his personal favourite — it guarantees the goal while eliminating the time element, so you are never at risk of losing the money. Make it conditional on key success actions: setting up a web page, attending calls, showing up to workouts, weighing in, reporting data. He reports that since advising businesses to use it, not a single client has taken one up; in practice either you happily keep working with a committed client to the result, or it quietly drops because the client is close enough to satisfied and the sales conversation is months in the past.

Modified service guarantee: give another Y-long period of service or access free, where Y is generally at least twice the original duration. This ties a specific duration to your extended involvement instead of being on the hook forever — a good starting point before the all-out service guarantee.
Credit-based guarantee: give back what they paid, but as credit toward any service you offer.

Outsized refund guarantee: double or triple their money back, or a no-strings payment far above the price, attached to a consumption condition. Fladlien's example: spend $X on ads using the course methods and if you do not make money, he buys the store for $25,000. He attributed an extra $3M in sales to it on a $2,997 course and only paid out 10 of the $25,000 refunds. This fits high-margin offers and situations where a lot must be done by the buyer and, if done, results are highly likely.
caveats: Outsized refund guarantees depend on high margins and a genuinely low chance of failure when conditions are met; the $25,000 payout is a case study, not a template for your economics.
The 'nobody claims the service guarantee' observation is the source's experience, not a statistical expectation.
Consumption conditions should reflect actions genuinely required for success, not gimmicks designed to disqualify buyers.

cards.title: Stacking Guarantees for Compounded Risk Reversal
cards.summary: Layer different guarantee types to remove risk sequentially and future-pace the buyer toward the outcome.
cards.use_when: Building a premium offer where a single guarantee is not enough to overcome hesitation.
steps: Layer an unconditional guarantee on top of a conditional one — e.g. a 30-day no-questions-asked refund plus a conditional triple-your-money-back 90-day guarantee.

Stack two conditional guarantees around sequential outcomes: you will make $10,000 by 60 days and $30,000 by 90 days, provided you do things 1, 2 and 3. Spelling out the conditional timeline future-paces the prospect into an outcome they now believe is far more likely.
Treat stacking as evidence you are serious about client results and convinced they will get them — it shifts risk from the buyer back onto you.
caveats: Stacked guarantees multiply your worst-case exposure; model the refund arithmetic from the risk-reversal math card before committing.
Future-pacing with specific dollar milestones sets expectations you must be prepared to honour.

cards.title: Crafting and Delivering an Unconditional Refund Guarantee
cards.summary: Pitch the strongest refund guarantee by removing the decision from today and promising to keep only happy money.
cards.use_when: Writing or delivering the guarantee portion of a webinar, sales page or closing conversation for a lower-ticket B2C offer.
steps: Remove the immediate yes/no: 'I am not asking you to decide yes or no today — I am asking you to make a fully informed decision.' Use the house analogy: you do not buy a house without looking inside, so get inside the program, verify the claims, and decide then.

Echo the source's phrasing: 'whether it is 29 minutes or 29 days from now — if you ain't happy, I ain't happy.' For any reason whatsoever, they can get the money back by emailing support with a simple request.
Back the promise with concrete support metrics if you have them — the original script cited average response times of 61 minutes over a 24/7 period.

Use a satisfaction-based guarantee with a best-case/worst-case close. Weight-loss program example: 'best case you get the body of your dreams; worst case you tell me I suck, I write you a check, and you get six weeks of free training. Both options are risk free — but the only thing guaranteed not to help you is walking out today.' He reports two people took him up on it out of 4,000 sales over three and a half years.

If you use satisfaction-based refunds, be genuinely good at fulfilment — the source credits the guarantee with a lot of closed deals but warns the model is riskier as ticket size and fulfilment cost rise.
caveats: Satisfaction/no-questions-asked is the highest form of guarantee because the buyer could ask for a refund even when you did everything right — the source says this works much better in lower-ticket situations.
His 2-in-4,000 refund rate is an example from his own business, not a benchmark.
Do not emit support response-time claims you cannot substantiate.

cards.title: Strengthening a Guarantee Through Naming and Wording
cards.summary: Give the guarantee a vivid, benefit-laden name and lead with the reason why, so it does not read as boilerplate.
cards.use_when: Finalising the wording and branding of a guarantee for sales copy or checkout messaging.
steps: Replace 'vanilla' terms like 'satisfaction' with a stronger, more concrete description.
Generic example to avoid: '30 Day Money Back Satisfaction Guarantee'.
Good creative imagery: 'In 30 days, if you would not jump into shark-infested waters to get our product back, we will return every dollar you paid.'
Even stronger: the source's 'Club a Baby Seal Guarantee' — after 30 days of using the services, if you would not club a baby seal to stay on as a customer, you do not pay a penny.
Always name the guarantee and state it boldly, with the reason why, even if you choose not to offer one.
caveats: The source's extreme imagery examples are intentionally provocative; tone must fit your brand and audience.
Verify advertising and refund-wording compliance for your market before publishing the named guarantee.
